The method for processing fermented or incubated cocoa beans comprises the steps of: adding water to fermented or incubated cocoa beans or nibs to form a suspension; wet grinding said suspension; subjecting said suspension to a heat treatment at a temperature of 70° C. or less; separating the suspension into a water phase (heavy phase), a fat phase (light phase) and a solid phase, said fat phase comprising cocoa butter as a major component and solids and/or water as minor components and said solid phase comprising cocoa powder and water; and separately processing the three phases, which comprises: neutralizing and/or removing acetic acid formed during fermentation or formed or added prior to or during an incubation of the cocoa beans via the water phase, and optionally separating cocoa butter from the fat phase, separating cocoa powder from the solid phase, and separating cocoa aroma and a polyphenolic powder from at least the water phase.

outputs.L2: A process for treating fermented or incubated cocoa beans includes the following operations: combining the fermented or incubated cocoa beans or nibs with water to produce a suspension; grinding that suspension in a wet state; applying heat to the suspension at a temperature not exceeding 70°C; dividing the suspension into three fractions: an aqueous fraction, or heavy phase; a lipid fraction, or light phase; and a solids fraction. The method relates to the processing of fermented or incubated cocoa beans or cocoa nibs. In this process, water is added to the beans or nibs in order to form an aqueous suspension. The addition of water facilitates subsequent mechanical treatment and enables the soluble and dispersible components of the cocoa material to be more effectively processed.

The suspension is then subjected to wet grinding. This step reduces the particle size of the cocoa material and helps release cocoa fat, soluble compounds, aroma precursors, polyphenols, and other constituents from the cellular structure of the beans or nibs. During or after wet grinding, the suspension is heat-treated at a temperature of 70° C. or less. Maintaining the temperature at or below this level helps preserve heat-sensitive cocoa components, such as aroma compounds and polyphenols, while still allowing effective processing of the suspension.

After wet grinding and heat treatment, the treated suspension is separated into different fractions. These fractions include a water phase, a fat phase, and a solid phase. The water phase contains water-soluble cocoa components and may also contain acids formed during fermentation or incubation, particularly acetic acid. The fat phase contains cocoa butter, while the solid phase includes non-fat cocoa solids and other particulate material.

The water phase may be used to neutralize or remove acetic acid that is generated during the fermentation or incubation of cocoa beans or nibs. By managing the acetic acid content, the method can improve the flavor profile of the cocoa material and reduce excessive acidity. This contributes to a milder and more balanced cocoa product.

The separated phases may also be subjected to further processing to obtain valuable cocoa-derived products. The fat phase can be refined or purified to produce cocoa butter. The solid phase can be dried, milled, and processed to produce cocoa powder. Components from the water phase may be recovered and concentrated to obtain cocoa aroma fractions or polyphenolic powders. In this way, the method allows the cocoa material to be fractionated into multiple useful products, including cocoa butter, cocoa powder, cocoa aroma, and polyphenolic powder, while preserving desirable flavor and nutritional components.
outputs.L4:
The method relates to the processing of cocoa beans, cocoa nibs, or comparable cocoa raw materials that have previously been fermented, incubated, or otherwise treated to develop cocoa flavor precursors. In this process, water is added to the cocoa material before or during size reduction, and the mixture is subjected to wet grinding. The presence of water during grinding allows the cocoa particles to be comminuted efficiently while creating an aqueous suspension in which water-soluble compounds can be released from the cocoa solids.

After wet grinding, the cocoa suspension is subjected to a heat treatment carried out at relatively low temperatures. This low-temperature treatment is selected so that undesirable volatile or water-soluble components, particularly acetic acid generated during fermentation, can be reduced, removed, or neutralized without causing excessive thermal damage to desirable cocoa flavor compounds, polyphenols, or other heat-sensitive constituents. The treatment conditions may be adjusted depending on the acidity of the cocoa material, the desired flavor profile, and the intended final products.

The treated suspension is then separated into distinct phases. Typically, these include an aqueous phase, a fat phase, and a solid phase. The aqueous phase contains dissolved acids, including acetic acid, as well as other water-soluble substances. By removing or treating this aqueous phase, the process reduces the acidity and harshness that can otherwise remain in cocoa products. Neutralization of the acetic acid may also be performed in or through the water phase, allowing acid control without directly degrading the cocoa fat or solid cocoa components.

The fat phase primarily contains cocoa butter. Because the separation is performed after wet grinding and controlled heat treatment, the cocoa butter can be recovered separately and may retain desirable sensory and functional properties. The solid phase contains cocoa solids that may be further processed, dried, milled, or refined to obtain cocoa powder or other cocoa-derived ingredients.

In addition to cocoa butter and cocoa powder, the method makes it possible to recover valuable aroma fractions and polyphenol-rich materials. Cocoa aroma compounds may be collected or concentrated from one or more of the phases, depending on the process configuration. Polyphenolic compounds, which are associated with antioxidant properties and contribute to the characteristic composition of cocoa, may be isolated or enriched to produce a polyphenolic powder.

Overall, the process provides a controlled way to transform fermented or incubated cocoa beans or nibs into multiple useful product streams. By using water addition, wet grinding, low-temperature heat treatment, and phase separation, the method enables effective management of acetic acid while preserving and separately recovering important cocoa components, including cocoa butter, cocoa powder, cocoa aroma, and polyphenol-containing powder.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” may be one of the smallest words in English, but it is also one of the most important. As a definite article, it helps us point to something specific. For example, when we say “the book,” we are not talking about any book, but a particular one that the speaker and listener both understand.

This simple word brings clarity and structure to sentences. It helps identify people, places, objects, and ideas. Without “the,” English would often sound vague or incomplete. Phrases like “the sun,” “the world,” and “the future” show how the word can refer to things that are familiar, unique, or meaningful.

Although “the” is easy to overlook, it plays a powerful role in communication. It reminds us that even the smallest words can have a big impact on how we understand language.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe an invention for treating cocoa beans or nibs using water suspension, wet milling, heat below 70°C, separation into heavy/light/solid phases, and separate recovery of cocoa butter, cocoa powder, aroma, and polyphenolic powder.
counterfactuals.output:
The invention relates to a process for treating cocoa beans, cocoa nibs, or cocoa bean fragments in an aqueous system to recover multiple cocoa-derived products while preserving heat-sensitive components.

In the process, cocoa material is mixed with water to form a suspension or slurry. The suspended cocoa material is then subjected to wet milling, grinding, or comminution, preferably under temperature-controlled conditions so that the temperature remains below about 70°C. This avoids excessive thermal degradation of aroma compounds, polyphenols, and other valuable cocoa constituents.

After wet milling, the resulting aqueous cocoa suspension is separated into distinct fractions, typically by centrifugation, decanting, filtration, or combinations of these techniques. The separation produces:

1. **A heavy phase**  
   This phase contains a substantial portion of cocoa solids and may include starches, proteins, cell wall material, and insoluble cocoa constituents.

2. **A light phase**  
   This phase is enriched in cocoa fat and is used for recovering cocoa butter. The cocoa butter may be separated from the aqueous portion by further centrifugation, skimming, clarification, or drying.

3. **An aqueous or liquid phase**  
   This phase contains water-soluble cocoa components, including aroma compounds, flavor precursors, sugars, acids, and polyphenolic substances.

4. **A solid phase**  
   Insoluble material from the cocoa may be recovered and processed into cocoa powder or cocoa powder ingredients.

The aqueous phase may be further treated to separately recover valuable cocoa aroma and polyphenolic fractions. Aroma compounds can be isolated by evaporation, stripping, distillation, membrane separation, adsorption, or condensation. Polyphenols can be concentrated and dried, for example by filtration, adsorption/desorption, membrane concentration, evaporation, freeze drying, or spray drying, to obtain a polyphenolic cocoa powder.

The solid cocoa fraction may be dried and milled to produce cocoa powder, while the fat-rich light phase yields cocoa butter. In this way, the invention enables separate recovery of cocoa butter, cocoa powder, cocoa aroma, and a polyphenol-rich cocoa powder from the same cocoa starting material.

A key advantage of the invention is that the cocoa is processed in water and at relatively low temperatures, below 70°C, thereby reducing loss of volatile aroma compounds and limiting degradation or oxidation of polyphenols. The process also allows efficient fractionation of cocoa into high-value components without relying on conventional high-temperature roasting or pressing as the primary separation method.

A method for processing cocoa beans or cocoa nibs, the method comprising:

1. combining cocoa beans and/or cocoa nibs with water to form an aqueous cocoa mixture;

2. wet grinding the aqueous cocoa mixture to produce a cocoa suspension;

3. heating the cocoa suspension to a temperature not exceeding 70°C;

4. separating the heated cocoa suspension into at least three phases comprising:
   - an aqueous phase;
   - a cocoa butter-containing phase; and
   - a cocoa solids-containing phase;

5. removing acetic acid from the aqueous phase.

In certain embodiments, the method further comprises isolating one or more cocoa-derived products selected from the group consisting of cocoa butter, cocoa powder, cocoa aroma compounds, and polyphenols.

In certain embodiments, the cocoa butter-containing phase is processed to recover cocoa butter.

In certain embodiments, the cocoa solids-containing phase is dried and/or milled to obtain cocoa powder.

In certain embodiments, volatile cocoa aroma compounds are recovered from the aqueous phase, the cocoa suspension, or a vapor phase generated during processing.

In certain embodiments, polyphenols are recovered from the aqueous phase and/or the cocoa solids-containing phase.

In certain embodiments, removal of acetic acid from the aqueous phase comprises evaporation, stripping, distillation, membrane separation, adsorption, extraction, neutralization, ion exchange, or any combination thereof.

In certain embodiments, the cocoa suspension is maintained at a temperature of 70°C or less during wet grinding, heating, and/or phase separation so as to preserve heat-sensitive cocoa constituents, including one or more of cocoa aroma compounds and polyphenols.

In certain embodiments, the water is added in an amount sufficient to facilitate wet grinding and phase separation of the cocoa beans and/or cocoa nibs into the aqueous phase, cocoa butter-containing phase, and cocoa solids-containing phase.
